clues.title: Pole: Pole marking
text: Black and yellow diagonal stripes on poles are common in South Korea. You might confuse them with Taiwanese ones, but in South Korea, the stripes never go all the way to the bottom, while the ones in Taiwan usually do and have more of an orange tint to them.

clues.title: Language: Language
text: Korean script is highly distinctive, featuring a combination of circular shapes and blocky, straight-line characters.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Jeju vulcanic rocks
text: Jeju is a volcanic island that has a lot of rock walls, made of dark volcanic rocks.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Road line: Roadlines
text: Roads have yellow middle lines and white outer lines.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Gimje Plain
text: The area around Gimje can be recognised by being one of the only completely flat areas of South Korea, combined with the open, yellow-green fields along almost every road in the area.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Jeju
text: Jeju is a volcanic island with a lot of dark volcanic dirt, where you can also often see volcanoes in the distance.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: General Landscape
text: The South Korean landscape is predominantly mountainous. It is very rare to not see at least some hills or mountains in the distance. Even in the flat areas, you can almost always see elevation on the horizon.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Coverage: Cars
text: Almost all road coverage in South Korea is made with a Generation 3 camera.
In most, but not all, of the coverage, the back of the Google car is visible.
**You can see three colours:**
Black, white and silver.
The car never has an antenna.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Coverage: Autumn & Winter
text: A considerable amount of the coverage was made during autumn and winter.
Note that more pleasant-looking spring and summer coverage is also not uncommon.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: Pole Sticker
text: Utility poles almost always have these pole markings near the bottom, consisting of black and yellow diagonal stripes.
**These markings look similar to the ones found in Taiwan. There are however two main differences:**
In South Korea, the stripes do not reach all the way to the bottom, whereas in Taiwan they do.
In South Korea, the stripes are more yellow. In Taiwan, they have more of an orange tint.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: Spike Pole
text: Most poles have a tapered “spike” on top.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Bollard: Bollard
text: You will sometimes see these black and white wedge-shaped bollards. They have a round yellow reflector on the front, and a grey one on the back.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Red Bricks
text: Red brick is a very common building material in South Korea.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Traditional Tiled Roofs
text: Many buildings have traditional tiled roofs like these.
These often have decorative elements on the corners, and tend to have sides that curve slightly upwards.
Blue roofs are quite common.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: South Korea
text: Area codes in South Korea increase to the south, from 02 in the north, to 064 on Jeju. It is also notable that Seoul has the only two-digit area code in the country.
